vignette: Mary, a 71-year-old forensic analyst, has recently experienced an assault that has left her grappling with intense psychological distress. Her daily life now is marked by moments of profound anxiety and avoidance behaviors, which she has come to rely on to cope with the traumatic event. The assault occurred at her workplace, where she was cornered in a storage room by a former colleague who had become increasingly erratic over time. The attack left her feeling violated and helpless, with specific triggers related to body parts associated with the event, making it difficult for her to process memories of that day fully. Mary often finds herself avoiding conversations about the future or any discussions related to the assault itself, as these topics trigger intense rage when she recalls what happened. Her memory of the incident is fragmented and emotionally charged; she feels a mix of intense anger and numbness, sometimes pushing away the memories before they can form completely. The partial recall leaves her feeling inadequate, reinforcing her belief that she cannot handle the trauma. This sense of inadequacy has led Mary to adopt several maladaptive coping strategies. She always sits with her back against a wall in public places, ensuring she can see everyone around her. This constant vigilance exacerbates her anxiety and reinforces her negative appraisals about her own vulnerability. Additionally, she has restricted her eating habits and avoids exercise altogether, believing that these actions will somehow protect her from further harm. Mary’s avoidance behaviors have also extended to her work environment. She now avoids the areas of the building where the assault took place and often skips important meetings or presentations where she might have to sit in a vulnerable position. Her relationship with her husband has also been strained, as he finds it difficult to understand her increased isolation and the way she shuts down emotionally. Her negative appraisals, such as feeling inadequate and believing that thinking about the event will make it unbearable, feed into her maladaptive strategies. She avoids exercise because she feels unable to face any physical exertion that might lead to thoughts of the assault. Similarly, her under-eating is a coping mechanism; by restricting food intake, she can momentarily distract herself from the memories and negative feelings. Mary’s memory fragmentation and the intense emotions it evokes have created a cycle where each trigger leads to another layer of distress. When she remembers parts of the event, she feels rage and numbness alternately, which further reinforces her negative appraisals about her ability to cope with life. This cycle has left her feeling increasingly isolated and miserable. Her husband’s concern over Mary’s deteriorating condition finally prompted her to seek help. She is most afraid that she will never regain the happiness she once had and worries that the memories will continue to haunt her indefinitely. Despite her fears, she hopes that therapy can provide a way to manage these overwhelming emotions and restore some semblance of normalcy in her life. Mary’s current state reflects a complex interplay between her triggers, maladaptive strategies, memory difficulties, and negative appraisals. Each component reinforces the others, creating a cycle of distress that has significantly impacted both her personal and professional life.
